result: MRSN performed WGS surveillance of 5129 P. aeruginosa isolates from 71 facilities (2011-2020), identifying 547 STs. ST-621 represented 5% of isolates but 89% originated from a single facility (Facility A) with high genetic relatedness (0-23 allelic differences by cgMLST). Patient transfers from Facility A were documented in 3 of 5 other facilities with ST-621, while 2 facilities had genetically distinct strains (88-89 allelic differences).
evaluation: Claims C1-C8 provide comprehensive surveillance data with specific counts, percentages, and genetic distance metrics. The data clearly establishes ST-621 as predominantly endemic to Facility A with documented evidence of patient transfers and genetic distinctness of isolates from other facilities. The cgMLST analysis provides robust genetic relatedness data.

result: Retrospective analysis identified 253 ST-621 isolates from Facility A (May 2011-December 2020) from 82 patients. All isolates belonged to a single outbreak clone with average genetic distance of 38 SNPs (IQR=19). The majority of isolates were from respiratory (42%) and urine (39%) samples. Most patients (56%) contributed serial isolates, with 6 patients showing prolonged carriage (exemplified by patient 35 with 21 urine isolates over 4.5 years).
evaluation: Claims C9-C19 provide detailed characterization of the outbreak with specific counts, percentages, and genetic metrics. The phylogenetic analysis with SNP distances and patient demographics are well-documented. The identification of prolonged carriage in specific patients with longitudinal sampling provides strong evidence for the outbreak's characteristics.

result: Two outbreak subclones (SC1 and SC2) were identified with distinct spatial and temporal distributions. SC1 (average 24 SNPs within subclone) was predominantly in the Main Building (78%) and detected before 2014 (60%), spreading mainly in ICUs/step-down units on floors 2-3 (wards 1-10). SC2 (average 31 SNPs within subclone) was predominantly in the Tower Building (52%) and detected after 2014 (77%), centered in ICUs on floor 3 (wards 20-21). Overall, ST-621 was observed in 26 wards/units across all 7 floors of both buildings.
evaluation: Claims C20-C30 provide comprehensive spatial-temporal analysis with specific percentages and genetic distances. The phylogenetic identification of two subclones with distinct distributions is well-supported by the data. The specific ward and floor locations with temporal patterns provide strong evidence for the distinct evolution and spread of the two subclones.

result: ER isolates were predominantly from urine cultures (92% vs 32% from other locations, p<0.0001) with 72% being serial isolates from returning patients. The epidemic curve showed an average of 11.5 new cases/year (2011-2016) declining to 3 cases/year (2017-2021). Overall P. aeruginosa cases at Facility A remained stable, though MRSN sampling was inconsistent due to staffing issues.
evaluation: Claims C31-C36 provide specific temporal trends with statistical significance and acknowledge sampling limitations. The ER pattern is well-characterized with significant p-value. The decline in outbreak cases is documented with specific numbers, and the manuscript appropriately acknowledges the sampling inconsistency as a limitation.

result: Molecular clock analysis dated the outbreak MRCA to 1999 (±3 years), shortly after the Main Building opened in 1996. Genetic diversity in 2011 (16.3 SNPs average) suggested earlier origin. SC1 and SC2 emerged concurrently with MRCAs in 2004 (±2 years), not as descendants. The first SC2 isolates were sampled after Tower Building opened in 2012, with the earliest from patient 27 (wound infection). Remarkably, 15 serial isolates from patient 27 (2012-2015) were not monophyletic, with MRCA coinciding with SC2 emergence.
evaluation: Claims C37-C46 provide robust temporal analysis using Bayesian molecular clock methods with confidence intervals. The dating of the outbreak origin and subclone emergence is well-supported by phylogenetic evidence. The non-monophyletic pattern in patient 27 with MRCA timing provides strong evidence for the early establishment of SC2 diversity.

result: SNP distribution analysis revealed unimodal distribution (peak 40.5) for all inter-patient isolates, but bimodal when filtered by same month/ward (lower peaks at 12.4, 15.3, 11.6 SNPs). Only 10 patients met criteria for presumed patient-to-patient transmission (all SC1, mostly 2011-2012, 6 in ICU #1 Main Building). Twelve cases met criteria for presumed environmental origin, including 3 patients in ICU #20 Tower Building with SC2 isolates differing by only 0-4 SNPs despite years apart (2015, 2016, 2018). Seven of nine most recent patients (2018-2020) had predicted environmental origin, including 5 cases from SC1 resurgence in ICUs #1-2.
evaluation: Claims C47-C56 provide detailed transmission inference based on SNP thresholds and epidemiological criteria. However, the manuscript explicitly acknowledges limitations: lack of detailed patient overlap data (C151-C152), conservative criteria leaving most cases undetermined (C154), and inability to distinguish direct transmission from healthcare worker-mediated transmission. The fixed threshold approach is acknowledged as a limitation requiring follow-up with probabilistic methods (C153-C154).

result: Environmental sampling (2021-2022) collected 159 swabs from 55 locations in 8 wards/units, confirming reservoirs of both SC1 and SC2 (n=17 isolates) in sink drains of 7 patient rooms in wards #1, 2, 6, and 20. During this period, 56 additional clinical isolates (25 SC1, 31 SC2) from 13 patients (including 11 new cases) were collected, indicating ongoing transmission.
evaluation: Claims C57-C61 provide direct environmental evidence supporting genomic inferences with specific counts and locations. The identification of sink drains as reservoirs with both subclones present, combined with concurrent detection of new clinical cases, provides strong evidence for ongoing environmental transmission. The sampling is contemporary and systematic.

result: Outbreak isolates showed multidrug resistance with temporal patterns. Imipenem non-susceptibility increased from 63% (2011) to >95% (2014+), while cefepime non-susceptibility decreased from 81% to 37% (2011-2014). These patterns correlated with SC1 decline and SC2 rise: SC2 showed significantly higher imipenem resistance (98% vs 76% SC1, p<0.001) and lower cefepime resistance (38% vs 66% SC1, p<0.001). Tobramycin and ciprofloxacin resistance remained highly prevalent and stable.
evaluation: Claims C62-C69 provide well-documented temporal resistance patterns with statistical significance. The correlation between resistance profiles and subclone dynamics is supported by chi-square tests with significant p-values. The phenotypic data aligns with the genotypic findings and phylogenetic patterns.

result: Outbreak isolates lacked plasmids and carried only two acquired resistance genes (crpP for ciprofloxacin, aac(6')-Ib4 for tobramycin) besides intrinsic AmpC β-lactamase. Analysis of 164 resistance-associated genes identified 68 distinct mutations (20 LOF) in 37 genes, with 8 genes mutated ≥3 times independently. OprD (carbapenem resistance) was most frequently mutated with 5/6 mutations being LOF, including R6* (115 SC2 isolates) and R318fs (92 SC1 isolates), predicted to occur 2006-2008 but SC2-OprD-R6* only became predominant from 2014. AmpD W97* LOF (>50 isolates, emerged 2012) and PBP3 R504C (>50 isolates, acquired independently twice in 2007 and 2014) were strongly associated with cephalosporin resistance.
evaluation: Claims C70-C86 provide comprehensive genomic analysis of resistance mechanisms with specific mutation counts, phylogenetic timing, and phenotypic associations. The absence of plasmids and acquired resistance genes is clearly stated. The temporal predictions from PAUP analysis are specific with dates. The independent acquisition of mutations and their associations with resistance phenotypes are well-documented.

result: Colistin resistance mutations were rare. NSY mutations in ColRS (3 sites, 4 isolates) and PmrAB (2 sites, 3 isolates) showed no MIC increase (4 mg/L, same as wild-type). However, Patient 2 (with colistin therapy history) acquired PhoQ E77fs LOF in 2 serial isolates, resulting in 8-fold MIC increase (32 mg/L). This colistin-resistant strain emerged in early 2011 but remained constrained to a single patient with no further spread detected.
evaluation: Claims C87-C93 provide specific mutation data with MIC values and patient information. The distinction between mutations with and without phenotypic effect is clear. The temporal emergence (2011) and lack of spread of the colistin-resistant strain is well-documented. The patient's treatment history provides context for the selection pressure.

result: Genome-wide analysis identified 64 genes with ≥2 independent mutations (excluding synonymous), functionally enriched for signal transduction (28% vs 6% genome-wide, p<0.001) and cell wall/membrane biogenesis (17% vs 7%, p=0.0017). Six cell wall genes (besides resistance genes) were recurrently mutated, including rmlA and betT2. Signaling genes included TCS (narXL, fleRS, cbrAB), with cbrAB most frequently mutated (16 NSY mutations in 80 isolates). Virulence regulators pvdS (6 NSY, 1 LOF), morA (11 NSY, 2 LOF), and mucAB (4 sites, 3 LOF) were also recurrently mutated.
evaluation: Claims C94-C102 provide comprehensive functional enrichment analysis with statistical significance. The specific gene counts and mutation types are well-documented. The enrichment in signal transduction and cell wall biogenesis is statistically significant and biologically relevant to adaptation. The identification of specific genes with mutation counts provides detailed evidence.

result: Pathway-level analysis showed significant enrichment of NSY/LOF mutations (vs. 0.11 sites/kb baseline) in Type IV secretion system (0.59 sites/kb, p<0.001), flagellar biosynthesis/chemotaxis (0.21 sites/kb, p=0.0264), alginate production (0.31 sites/kb, p=0.0088), and O-antigen production (0.36 sites/kb, p=0.0126). Notably, WbpX (O-antigen biosynthesis) was disrupted (S19fs) in 127 SC2 isolates, with PAUP predicting this occurred in 2005 (±24 months), concomitant with SC2 emergence.
evaluation: Claims C103-C108 provide rigorous statistical analysis of pathway enrichment with specific mutation densities and p-values. The WbpX disruption in SC2 is well-documented with specific isolate counts and temporal prediction from phylogenetic analysis. The timing coinciding with SC2 emergence provides strong evidence for its role in subclone differentiation.

result: SC2 was associated with long-term infections: 5/6 patients with >1 year infections (9/11 for >6 months) carried SC2. All but one SC2 isolate carried truncated WbpX (essential for CPA biosynthesis). Convergent mutations in genes for alginate production, quorum-sensing deficiency, loss of motility, and decreased protease secretion (all chronic infection-associated phenotypes) were observed throughout 10 years of sampling.
evaluation: Claims C137-C143 provide strong association between SC2 and long-term infections with specific patient counts. The WbpX truncation prevalence in SC2 is well-documented. The convergent evolution toward chronic infection-associated phenotypes is supported by specific gene categories with citation support for their association with chronic infections.

result: The Main and Tower Buildings of Facility A have distinct plumbing systems, providing ecological separation for the spread and divergence of the two subclones (aside from inter-hospital patient transfers).
evaluation: Claims C144-C145 provide a clear mechanistic explanation for the spatial-temporal separation of subclones. The distinct plumbing systems provide physical infrastructure supporting the observed epidemiological patterns. This is consistent with the environmental reservoir data and subclone distributions.

result: The study had several acknowledged limitations: (1) partial and inconsistent sampling prevented capturing exact outbreak magnitude and introduced potential sampling bias; (2) detailed epidemiological data (admission dates, bed locations, medications) were unavailable; (3) patient overlaps were only inferred from location and culture dates, with many likely undetected; (4) fixed thresholds for transmission inference were conservative, leaving most case origins undetermined. Alternative probabilistic methods (TransPhylo) are being explored in follow-up studies.
evaluation: Claims C150-C154 provide transparent acknowledgment of study limitations. The manuscript explicitly recognizes the constraints of retrospective analysis, incomplete epidemiological data, and conservative inference criteria. The mention of follow-up work with probabilistic methods demonstrates appropriate scientific rigor in acknowledging methodological limitations.

result: Study findings led to ongoing interventions at Facility A (closing sinks, replacing tubing, foaming detergents) and implementation of near real-time WGS surveillance of all P. aeruginosa isolates (not just MDR) starting in 2021. As of May 2025, no new ST-621 cases were reported for >15 months, with only 4 cases identified in 2022-2024, confirming slowed transmission.
evaluation: Claims C158-C161 provide concrete evidence of study impact with specific interventions and surveillance changes. The temporal data on case reduction (no new cases for >15 months, only 4 cases in 2022-2024) provides strong evidence for intervention effectiveness. The implementation of comprehensive surveillance demonstrates practical application of findings.

result: The manuscript provides comprehensive background on P. aeruginosa as an opportunistic pathogen causing infections in high-risk patients (CF, burns, neutropenia) with high morbidity/mortality. CRPA accounts for 16-30% of US cases and is categorized as a 'critical' pathogen. P. aeruginosa develops resistance primarily through chromosomal mutations in hundreds of genes (mutational resistome), with well-characterized mechanisms including GyrAB (fluoroquinolones), PBP3 (cephalosporins), Mex efflux systems, OprD inactivation (carbapenems), and PhoPQ (polymyxins). The pathogen possesses extensive virulence factors (T4P, LPS, exotoxins, flagellum, TSSs) regulated by TCSs, with biofilm formation key to persistence in patients and hospital water environments, leading to increasing outbreak reports linked to contaminated sinks/drains/taps.
evaluation: Claims C109-C128 provide well-cited background information establishing the clinical and public health significance of P. aeruginosa. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to established literature. This background contextualizes the study's importance and provides necessary scientific foundation.

result: Traditional outbreak detection approaches may miss comparable outbreaks due to sporadic infections, scattered cases, and changing resistance profiles. Surveillance programs targeting 'high-risk' isolates with specific resistance genes (ESBLs, carbapenemases) would fail to detect the ST-621 outbreak clone. While ST-621 was previously studied as a blaIMP-13-carrying epidemic clone in Europe (with sporadic detection in South America/Southeast Asia), the IMP-carrying strain has not been reported in the USA, and the Facility A outbreak represents a distinct MDR clone lacking carbapenemase. Healthcare networks with prospective WGS surveillance are reporting large numbers of unrecognized outbreaks.
evaluation: Claims C129-C135 provide important context for why this outbreak was initially undetected and distinguish it from previously described ST-621 strains. The limitations of traditional and targeted surveillance are well-articulated with citation support. The distinction from the European IMP-carrying strain is clearly established, and the trend of WGS revealing unrecognized outbreaks is appropriately cited.

result: Sinks with shallow basins and gooseneck faucets (like those in Facility A) have been linked to increased backsplash. A recent study showed sinks in a newly built ICU were contaminated with P. aeruginosa before patient arrival. The R504C PBP3 substitution has been linked to ceftazidime/avibactam resistance. OprD mutations are among the most common mechanisms for carbapenem resistance. The emergence of colistin resistance demonstrates that extensively drug-resistant P. aeruginosa is 'only a prescription and a few mutations away.'
evaluation: Claims C136, C146-C149 provide relevant contextual information from the literature with appropriate citations. These claims support the interpretation of findings and place them in broader context of P. aeruginosa hospital epidemiology and resistance evolution. All statements are appropriately cited.

result: TransPhylo uses probabilistic models to predict transmission and reconstruct transmission trees, recently extended to allow multiple genomes per host and incorporate epidemiological data. Routine WGS surveillance has potential to improve patient care and prevent some of the estimated 136 million hospital-associated drug-resistant infections per year globally.
evaluation: Claims C155-C157, C162-C163 provide appropriate context for future work and broader implications. The description of TransPhylo is accurately cited, and the global burden estimate is appropriately referenced. The potential impact statement is reasonable given the study's demonstration of WGS utility.

result: MRSN requested all MDR isolates (≥3 antibiotic families) from US facilities (2011-2020) with variable compliance, collecting 5129 isolates from 71 facilities (1511 from Facility A). Starting 2021, all P. aeruginosa isolates (MDR or not) were requested from Facility A. Pangenome analysis showed core genome (≥99% isolates) of 5674 genes, shell genome (≥95%) of 297 genes, and cloud genome (≥15%) of 530 genes. Genome-wide mutation analysis identified 629 mutated sites (257 singletons, 372 shared by ≥2 isolates) in 488 genes.
evaluation: Claims C164-C170 provide essential methodological details about sampling strategy, collection numbers, and genomic analysis. The specific gene counts for pangenome components and mutation analysis are clearly stated. The acknowledgment of variable compliance is appropriate transparency about data collection.
